# 00. Method Overview: How GPC Thinks About This Work

Source: 8/24/2026 Rush Enterprises call set (4 discovery interviews, 1 internal GO call, 1 client check-in) and 8/25/2026 Rush call set (4 functional-team interviews, 1 internal debrief).

Citation tags used below point at files in `transcripts/2026-08-24-rush/`: **[kevin]** = interview-gm-group-2-kevin, **[gm-1]** = interview-gm-group-1-jesse-ryan, **[peterbilt]** = interview-rgm-peterbilt-justin-hal, **[intl]** = interview-rgm-international-garrett-boston-adam, **[go]** = go-call-internal, **[check-in]** = checkin-lacy-marcelo — and at files in `transcripts/2026-08-25-rush/`: **[parts]** = interview-parts-joe-kyle-jeremy-shivniel, **[aftermarket]** = interview-aftermarket-chad-victor-deborah-mike, **[it]** = interview-it-asif-daniel-matthias, **[reporting]** = interview-reporting-jeff-marcus-robin-joshua-isaac, **[debrief]** = debrief-internal-grant-olivia — and at `transcripts/2026-08-26-delta-water-products/`: **[delta-go]** = go-call-internal — and at `transcripts/2026-08-27-rush/`: **[sales]** = interview-sales-will-steven-adam-marcelo — and at `transcripts/2026-08-19-rush/`: **[kickoff]** = kickoff-leadership.md (cite the timestamped body only), **[kickoff-agenda]** = kickoff-agenda-prep.md — and at `transcripts/2026-07-15-delta-water-products/`: **[delta-data]** = data-review-call.md (pre-SOW sales call). Anything marked **[inferred]** was reasoned from the transcripts rather than observed in them.

## The core philosophy

**Start with the people, not the technology.** All four interviews open with a version of "we start with the people." The fullest statement of why comes from the Kevin call: "we start with the people because ultimately the people are not going anywhere and we want AI to be a complement, not a replacement. We're not believers in subtraction. We believe in multiplication of human effort." **[kevin]** The subtraction and multiplication line appears only on that call; the other three carry the shorter version, and the International call pairs it with "AI is just a tool, just like Excel." **[intl]**

This is not just positioning. It shapes the entire method:

- Discovery interviews barely mention AI. Grant says it directly: "That's why I rarely talk about AI in these calls, because that's not the focus. The focus is, where are the things that drain your time and energy?" **[kevin]**
- Infrastructure comes before intelligence. "If you have AI reading bad data, you're not going to get a good answer." **[kevin]** The ordering he walks clients through is data cleanliness and integrity, then automation, then AI, then better forecasting and better decisions: "That is pre-AI. That is just automation. And before automation, it's data cleanliness and integrity. And data cleanliness and integrity gets us better forecasting so we can make better decisions." **[gm-1]**
- Some problems are human problems. When Kevin described teams bypassing process, Grant tested it as a lanes problem rather than a technology problem ("so it's like we're not staying in our lanes in a way? Like the lanes aren't well-defined?") and Kevin agreed. **[kevin]** The method leaves room for a finding that the fix is process rather than software.
- The bar being set is reliability, not novelty. "We want it to be as reliable as a tool like Excel, effectively." **[gm-1]** The comparison recurs on the International call: "AI is just a tool, just like Excel," and again on the check-in, where the adoption goal is stated as getting people to "trust this tool like they trust Excel within reason." **[intl] [check-in]** On 8/25 the Excel frame comes back from the client's side: Mike Eppes argues that locking down AI is like refusing people Excel "because they might write the wrong formula in it," and Grant extends it — deterministic math has one answer reached different ways, AI has different answers too, "but we want people to rely on it like in Excel, but we also need IT to feel comfortable about that, which is the trick." **[aftermarket]**

The infrastructure-first rule has a pre-SOW instance too. On the Delta data review call Grant asked the uncomfortable question on purpose ("I've got a question for you that might be uncomfortable but it's worth asking... Do you trust the reports or would you say that your lieutenants trust the reports that are in HubSpot?"), got a no, and set the boundary before any scope existed: deal stages accurate, clear definitions of when they move, what is required to mark closed won. "This is table stakes. We won't touch anything else without doing that." **[delta-data 18:02]** He offered the escape hatch in the same breath: pre-meeting and post-meeting workflows "don't necessarily need HubSpot to be flawless," so quick wins can run beside the data cleanup. The adoption logic he attached to that is the same trust ladder stated as a flywheel: "quick wins, which tell stories, generate curiosity. Curiosity then creates new exploration and new wins." **[delta-data 23:54]**

**Probleming before solutioning.** Grant named the origin of the whole discovery posture on the IT call, quoting his own trainer: "Grant, you keep on jumping to solutioning in your second question. You need to do more probleming first." That is why an interview runs an hour without proposing anything: "we're happy without proposing any solutions because that's not the goal of this call." **[it]** The client-facing version of the same rule, from the Parts call: "it's not about you guys knowing what's technically possible. It's about us knowing what would make your lives easier, and then we'll take care of the technicals." **[parts]**

## The four questions of work

Every workflow assessment decomposes work the same way. How is work:

1. Created
2. Delegated
3. Completed
4. Marked as complete

If you can answer those four for any role, you can find where copy-paste, manual steps, and information routing live, and that's where the opportunities are. All four 8/24 interviews state these four questions in the opening monologue **[kevin] [gm-1] [peterbilt] [intl]**, and they recur on the 8/25 monologues too **[parts] [aftermarket] [it]** (the Reporting transcript starts mid-call, so its opening is unverifiable).

## Pro Dreamer / Pro Complainer

The two framing stances for every interview:

- **Pro Complainer:** "What are the things that drain your time and energy?" Always asked first, on all four interviews.
- **Pro Dreamer:** the magic wand question. Kevin's version: "what does it look like in your role if you wave a magic wand and all your dreams come true?" **[kevin]** On the Peterbilt call he sharpens it by removing the technology from the frame first: "if you were to believe a magic wand, take AI out of the picture. My concern is not telling you what AI can do." **[peterbilt]**

By 8/27 the process-therapist frame — which entered the repertoire on 8/24 as a pickup of the client's own joke (see module 01, "Name the emotion, lightly") — has migrated into the opening monologue itself, attached to the complainer stance: "I say complaining willingly, because people think of us as their kind of process therapists, I want you guys to complain about the things that drain your time and energy, because then if I remove those from your plate, you'll want to have another call." **[sales]** A line a client handed him one day is standard kit three days later.

Why complainer first: "if I can remove those things off of your plate fast, then I know that you're going to like me and you're going to give me more problems to solve." **[intl]** Quick wins buy trust, trust buys access, access surfaces the bigger opportunities. This is a trust ladder, not a survey. On 8/25 he says the rationale out loud to the clients themselves, on every call where the monologue is captured: "if I can get those things off your plate, there's a very good chance you'll want to have another call with us... that means that we're doing something right." **[parts] [aftermarket] [it]** He also tells rooms explicitly to go to the extremes: "We love knowing the extremes because that's how we're able to make meaningful change. The stuff in between, the small stuff is interesting to us, but it's not the needle mover." **[parts]**

## The value math

Every opportunity gets sized the same way: **average hourly rate × frequency × duration = time or money saved.** That's the business-case lens. Grant named two more lenses on the check-in call, calling all of them "the three main pursuits that we have": constraint-focused (find the bottleneck in the business and ease it, even with small improvements) and business-goal-focused (take the quarter's goal, find everyone it touches, and aim AI at making that goal land faster). **[check-in]** Know which lens the client is buying with before you pitch an opportunity.

On 8/25 the time-math got a clean, teachable form he uses in the room to make interviewees rank their own work: "the largest value multiple, which means the time it takes you to do it, the frequency at which you do it. So one monthly report that takes you eight hours, it would have an answer of eight, versus something that takes you three hours every week would be 12." **[reporting]** Monthly hours-per-month is the unit; the bigger number wins. And when a dollar figure exists, chase it until it's spoken: the no-move inventory thread on the Parts call ends with Joe sizing it unprompted — "it's a very big opportunity, about a $20 million opportunity" — and Grant marking the target: "I like those numbers. I would like to impact those numbers." **[parts]**

The business-goal lens — previously only described on the check-in — is observed working in the room on 8/27. Steven volunteers the 2030 market-share goal (heavy-duty ~6.4% → 7.5%, medium-duty → 6.4%, ~6,500 trucks each), Grant does the addition out loud and marks it — "Combined, it's 13,000 trucks" — and then wires the day's findings to it: the untapped-market thread ("there's five accounts in LA that are, that are huge accounts and that's what they live off of... There's another 8,000 trucks") becomes, within two minutes, a demo request anchored to the goal ("If I asked for an export of your current account list for one of the demos that we prepare in LA, would that be feasible?"). **[sales]** Take the client's stated goal, restate its size in units they count in, then attach opportunities to it — that is the business-goal lens executed, not just named.

The sales-call version of the value math adds the tracking half: "When we automate something, we ask someone, how long does it take? And then we understand what's their salary and how frequently does it happen? We can project that out into a business case. And then when the automation is turned on, we calculate and track every automation run." **[delta-data 22:27]** And a question that belongs at the top of any engagement, asked here of both sponsors: "When I ask you what does productivity mean... what comes to your mind? What are your definitions?" **[delta-data 13:17]** The two answers differed (Madhav: less time on redundant tasks; Larry: build a business of value and widen the moat, "not efficiencies... all day long") **[delta-data 16:10, 16:33]**, which is the point of asking: it tells you which of the three lenses each sponsor is buying with.

## Scope discipline

The value math has a mirror image at engagement scale: better to win one slice than to lose the whole. When Delta's 10-hour SOW met a multi-brand portfolio, the GO call answer was focus — "If we try to go for everything, we're not going to get anything done. Each brand is going to have their own stack, their own problems, their own magic moments" — with the multiplication deferred, not abandoned: "one portfolio, one CFO, one president to convince, but multiple retainers... every brand should get their own workflow assessment." **[delta-go]** Land small, prove it, replicate. The same trust-ladder logic as Pro Complainer, applied to contracts instead of questions.

## The technology ladder

Not everything needs AI, and saying so builds credibility. The three upper rungs come from the International RGM call, where Grant drew the line explicitly while summarizing Boston's WIP problem. **[intl]** The bottom rung comes from the GM and Kevin calls, where he put data cleanliness and lane definition underneath automation. **[gm-1] [kevin]** The table below is assembled from those calls; the four-rung presentation is the playbook's own framing **[inferred]**.

| Layer | What it is | Example from 8/24 | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Process fix | Humans agree on lanes, stages, and required fields | Defining the Rush sales stages and handoffs | **[gm-1] [kevin]** |
| Automation | Deterministic logic, if-this-then-that, no intelligence needed | Status A plus status B mismatch routes to the parts back-counter person | **[intl]** |
| AI workflow | A model reads unstructured content inside a defined flow | Reading tech notes and last-update text, then confirming or updating status | **[intl]** |
| Intelligence layer | General reasoning across systems and history | Anomaly detection plus a drafted email to the right person | **[intl] [peterbilt]** |

When Boston proposed training an AI model to catch status conflicts, Grant took the deterministic half of the problem back off the AI pile in the same breath: "There's no AI in that. There should not be any AI in that because that does not need an intelligent layer on top. That's just a logic question." **[intl]** The same de-escalation shows up on the Parts call when ticket hygiene comes up: required fields "are things that actually don't have anything to do with AI. They're more systematic or infrastructure level, but we know that they're going to make an impact because it's just reducing one more email." **[parts]**

## Exception management (the day-two synthesis)

By the end of the functional-team interviews a single cross-org frame had emerged, and Grant started narrating it back to rooms as his working thesis. The pieces:

- **Dashboards are informational, not actionable.** Joe Duncan, on the Parts corporate dashboard his managers spend up to half a day digging through: "this dashboard is just informational... All we're doing is giving them the information. It is up to them of what is the next piece of action... it's missing the action." **[parts]**
- **Managers want to manage by exception.** Marcus: "we're not helping the managers manage by exception... the ideal state is we tell you, hey, this is what you need to look at today." Jeff: "It needs to be exception-based reporting. What actions can I take today to course correct before this becomes a bigger problem?" **[reporting]**
- **Grant's replay of the frame:** "I'm seeing a lot of exception management... if we can go and find those signals of exceptions before they hit the age where they become a problem," with the concrete shape of "a Monday scheduled task that says, hey, let's do an exception check in warranty, let's do an exception check in CRM..." **[reporting]**

The generalized pattern to listen for in any client: report → human interpretation → manual routing → action. Every stage after "report" is opportunity, and the highest-value target is the gap between *knowing* and *acting*. Root-cause chasing is the deeper version of the same thing — Mike Eppes: "we need to focus more on the root causes versus the daily groundhog day of firefighting." **[aftermarket]**

## Theory and action (how findings get bucketed)

At the close of the IT call Grant consolidated the whole engagement's needs into two buckets, and the debrief confirmed it as the strategy skeleton: the **theory** bucket (AI strategy, governance policy, bottoms-up innovation pipeline, onboarding people to the AI plan) and the **action** bucket (help desk, training, token monitoring, MCP and skill repository, internal AI marketing, continuous discovery interviewing). **[it] [debrief]** When a day of interviews produces a pile of findings, sort them into those two buckets before writing anything client-facing.

## The trust mechanics

Two lines from the check-in that reveal how he thinks about the engagement itself:

- "transcript plus asset equals knowledge." **[check-in]** Interviews give you the words, the client's real files give you the material. You need both before you build anything.
- Deliverables are proof, not decoration. The demo chosen at the end of the day was picked because it solves a pain a named stakeholder said out loud, hours earlier, on a recorded call. **[check-in]**

## Governance posture (citizen developers)

From the check-in call, GPC's stance on employees who build their own tools (like Jesse's Copilot agents): let them build. Do not put a form in front of the first spark. Grant's read on a competing firm's intake-form approach: "I think that that completely shuts down the magic and the wonder and the excitement around this technology." **[check-in]** The form, the security review, and the engineering resources come at the hardening stage, when a tool has proven value and multiple people want it: "at that point, when we need enterprise resources from an engineering team or the security and compliance team, that's when a form is more applicable." **[check-in]** The path is individual builds it, value shows, others want it, then enterprise-grade security and deployment. Watch for these builders in interviews. They are your best demo material and your best internal champions.

Worth holding alongside this: Rush's own corporate AI team had already built the opposite thing, an opportunity intake form asking for the current problem, the goal, and the expected benefit, which Marcelo described and then asked Grant to grade. **[check-in]** Grant validated the instinct to structure and size opportunities without endorsing the form as the entry point. The posture is not anti-form, it is anti-form-first.

The 8/25 IT call filled in the client's side of this picture and sharpened GPC's rule. Daniel Decker's team has a form *plus* an agent that iterates a one-page idea into a 10–20 page PRD-grade document with KPIs tied to corporate strategy — Grant probed it rather than grading it ("how far did you guys get into designing that intake funnel?"), asked to see the form and agent instructions, and offered a comparison against GPC's own makemyprd.com tool. **[it]** And he stated the hardening threshold crisply: a self-built skill or artifact that only benefits its builder and runs on read-only access "can stay in your local environment... it's really a token problem. But as soon as someone else finds value in that thing, that's where we need to start having the conversation of how do we enterprise or harden that skill." **[it]** Read-only plus single-user equals leave it alone; shared value equals harden it. That is the governance line in one sentence.

Why the citizen builders matter politically, from the debrief: "The fact that all of leadership knows who Jesse is, is a pretty big deal." **[debrief]** A builder whose name executives already know is a governance case study the client has pre-sold to itself.

The 8/27 sales call added the scale-up rule in Grant's own plain arithmetic, delivered to a builder in the room (Will Waterbury, who has working Claude prompts for CRM-scorecard coaching and competitor-pricing sourcing): "as soon as it's providing value to you, and then we see it would also provide value to Adam. We go, all right, that's two, two makes a party. Let's send it up the ladder... And then we can help roll that out to the entire company." **[sales]** One user is a local tool; a second user is the trigger for the pipeline. Note also that the builder himself asked for the guardrails — "we don't want to give them a sandbox just to play in. I want to tee up stuff and can things I can give them" — and for training ("if I could... be educated on how to get better, utilize less tokens"). **[sales]** Distribution discipline and token-efficiency coaching are things the good builders *want*; offering them is not a restriction, it is the ask being answered.

The same exchange shows the broker posture between builders and IT, stated to the client's face: "I know because we're also talking to IT that that is going to get cut because they're saying you need to access CRM data. I don't trust you slash the system... So one of the things that we're working on in our proposal is here's a governance structure for what we would call bottoms up innovation." **[sales]** Naming the other department's objection before it lands does two things: it proves GPC is triangulating across the org, and it converts a future veto into a requirement the proposal already answers.
